title: Do Bug-Repellent Paint Additives Actually Work?
description: Insect-inhibiting paint additives get a lot of hype in humid Houston. Here's an honest look at what they can and can't do — and what actually keeps bugs out.
author: Chris Petkau
imageAlt: Freshly painted brick home exterior in Sugar Land, TX by The Proud Paintbrush
content:
If you live anywhere around Houston, you already know the bugs never really clock out. So it's no surprise that one of the questions we get on exterior jobs is some version of: "Can't you just put something in the paint to keep them away?" Insect-inhibiting paint additives are real products, and they come up a lot in our humid climate. Here's a straight, hype-free look at what they actually do.

What Insect-Inhibiting Paint Additives Are

These are products designed to be mixed into paint before application, marketed to discourage insects from settling on treated surfaces — typically exterior walls, eaves, and soffits where bugs like to gather. They're sold as a supplement to a normal coating, not a special paint on their own.

One honest caveat worth stating plainly: the specific active ingredients, how long they stay effective, and exactly which insects they affect vary by product, and manufacturers' claims aren't all created equal. We'd encourage any homeowner to read the product label, confirm it's registered for its intended use, and treat broad "kills every bug" marketing with healthy skepticism. We don't make efficacy claims about any particular additive — we follow the manufacturer's directions and set realistic expectations.

What They Realistically Can — and Can't — Do

The fair way to think about an additive is as one small layer of help, not a force field. At best, it may make a treated exterior surface less inviting for insects to land on or congregate around. What it is not is a replacement for keeping pests out of your home: it won't seal the gaps they crawl through, treat a nest, or address an active infestation. Expecting paint to do a pest-control company's job is how homeowners end up disappointed.

Where an Additive Makes the Most Sense

If you do want to try one, the exterior is where it's most relevant — shaded eaves, porch ceilings, and north-facing walls where bugs and mildew both like to settle. While you're at it, a clean surface matters far more than any additive: starting from a properly washed wall is what makes any coating perform, which is why we treat pressure washing as the foundation of every exterior painting project. A great additive over a chalky, dirty wall is wasted money.

The Real Fix: Pair Paint With Actual Pest Control

If insects are genuinely a problem at your house, the durable solution isn't in the paint can — it's a proper pest-control program plus sealing the entry points around your foundation, windows, and eaves. A local company like Texas A1 Pest Control can actually identify what you're dealing with and treat it, which does far more than any additive can on its own. Think of a paint additive, if you use one at all, as a minor complement to that — never the front line.

How We Handle Additives on a Job

We're happy to incorporate a manufacturer-approved additive into your exterior coating when you ask for it, mixed at the correct ratio and applied per the label so it doesn't compromise the paint's finish or adhesion. What we won't do is oversell it.
